/MONDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 201 PM CST Sun Nov 1 2026

Monday/Tuesday...deep low pressure will settle in southern South 
Dakota early in the day Monday with a crashing cold front exiting 
eastern Wyoming. With an influx of cooler air from modest Canadian 
high pressure over the northern Rockies, temperatures will likely 
fall quickly through the remainder of the day. Though some questions 
remain about timing of the said frontal passage, most NWP guidance 
generally agrees it'll be before Noon for areas west of Highway 83 
and by mid afternoon for areas to the east. With a deep surface low 
falling below the 5th percentile in NAEFS climatology, increased 
kinematics resulting from a tight pressure gradient will promote 
strong cold air advection. This will lead to falling temperatures 
for most of the day west of Highway 83 as gusts ramp up markedly. 
Expectation is for gusts to increase to 30+ mph for these areas with 
a delayed onset of the stronger winds to the east. As the frontal 
boundary progresses south and east, it'll encounter richer moisture 
within the warm sector where instability should be more readily 
available. The NAM12 solution paints localized areas of 1000 j/kg 
MUCAPE within a strongly sheared environment. This would support a 
strong to potentially severe thunderstorm threat but confidence in 
where storms initiate on the boundary remains low. The latest SPC 
Day 2 Outlook keeps any severe threat east of the area, which aligns 
with HREF probabilities. That said, the NAM12 and HRRR solutions 
prog a further west frontal position which would introduce a greater 
thunderstorm threat for our eastern zones in central Nebraska. This 
will need to be closely monitored going forward. Rain will continue 
further northwest beneath the deformation band with greater QPF/PoPs 
limited to South Dakota and closer to the Pine Ridge/far western 
Sandhills. While precipitation will continue overnight Monday into 
Tuesday as temperatures fall, it's believed that the fall should be 
slow enough to preclude anything but rain as the predominant 
precipitation type. Interestingly, the RAP13 suggests some potential 
for a mix in our far western zones (west of Highway 61), but this 
remains fairly uncertain for now. By early Tuesday, a dynamic 
vertically stacked system should be in place over eastern Nebraska. 
With western Nebraska on the back edge of this system, winds will 
become the primary concern. Wind gusts should increase through late 
Monday/early Tuesday where ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index (EFI) values 
climb to around 0.6-0.8 with non-zero Shift of Tails (SoT) values. 
NBM hourly gust probabilities reach 60-80% of exceeding 41 knots by 
Monday evening with further increasing spatial coverage by Tuesday. 
Though probabilities decrease notably when upping to 48+ knot 
probabilities, BUFKIT soundings show efficient momentum transfer 
potential beneath a belt of h85 flow pushing 40-45 knots. Do believe 
consideration should be given to High Wind Watches with later 
forecasts as 50 knot gusts cannot be ruled out at this time. While 
some diurnal bump in temperatures appears possible Tuesday, it's 
unlikely to be overly significant and thus high temperatures for the 
day will likely occur early with values only in the middle 40s to 
lower 50s. As the main h5 low stalls over eastern Nebraska, 
precipitation should linger for west central through eastern 
Nebraska and only once the low begins to weaken/track away do winds 
diminish and PoPs decrease. Low temperatures will continue to fall 
and should approach the freezing mark Tuesday night for our western 
areas but settle in the upper 30s for all other locations to the 
east.

Wednesday and beyond...convoluted pattern in the extended. Active 
northern stream jet should settle south again with a secondary low 
crossing out of Colorado by Thursday/Friday. This southern track 
will likely carry with it most if not all precipitation potential 
with it and this is echoed well with the NBM 90th percentile QPF 
output which maintains dry conditions locally. A steady stream of 
disturbances will train from the Pacific Northwest through the Great 
Lakes for the late week and while this will keep synoptic lift 
absent to the north, trailing frontal boundaries should lead to 
slightly varying temperatures and low end precipitation chances. The 
model blend paints Slight Chance (< 25%) PoPs Saturday into Sunday 
for the area though individual EPS/GEFS outputs show fairly low 
probabilities themselves for measurable moisture so expect some 
adjustments with subsequent forecasts.
